text: Ako Adjei (17 June 1916 – 14 January 2002) was a Ghanaian statesman, politician, lawyer, and journalist. He was a founding member of the United Gold Coast Convention (UGCC) and one of the six leaders detained during Ghana's struggle for independence from Britain, a group known as The Big Six. Adjei became a member of parliament as a Convention People's Party (CPP) candidate in 1954 and held ministerial offices until 1962, when he was wrongfully detained as Minister for Foreign Affairs following the Kulungugu bomb attack. Born in Adjeikrom, a small farming community in the Akyem Abuakwa area of the Eastern Region of Ghana (then the Gold Coast), Adjei’s father was Samuel Adjei, a farmer and trader, and his mother was Johanna Okaile Adjei, both from La near Accra. He had many siblings but was the youngest of his father’s children. His early education began at the Busoso Railway Primary School, where he walked 14 miles each day, followed by studies at the La Presbyterian Junior and Senior Schools. In March 1933, he won a scholarship to Christ Church Grammar School, but returned to the La Presbyterian Senior School after a month due to disliking the environment. He then entered the Accra Academy in April 1933, where he walked four miles to school and passed the Junior Cambridge examination in 1934. In December 1936, he passed the Cambridge Senior School Leaving Certificate Examination, one of only two students exempted from the London Matriculation Examination Board. While at the Accra Academy, he developed an interest in journalism and wrote for the African Morning Post, a newspaper owned by Nnamdi Azikiwe. Azikiwe arranged for him to study at Lincoln University, Pennsylvania, where he lived at Houston Hall and played football. He shared a room with K. A. B. Jones-Quartey and was adjacent to Kwame Nkrumah’s room, with whom he formed a close relationship. They frequently held discussions about African decolonization, including with Ozuomba Mbadiwe, Nwafor Orizu, and Ikechukwu Ikejiani. After one and a half years, he won a Phelps-Stokes Fund scholarship to attend Hampton Institute, then transferred to Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism, earning a master’s degree in June 1943. He later became a lecturer at Fisk University through Dr. Edwin W. Smith, who invited him to assist in establishing the African Studies Department. To pursue a law career, Adjei moved to the United Kingdom, enrolling at the Inner Temple in May 1944. His father leased a family house in Accra to a Lebanese merchant for £10 per year for 50 years, with 30 years’ rent paid in advance, though the deal was completed after his father’s death and signed by Adjei and his brothers. In Britain, he became active in colonial politics and joined the West African Students Union (WASU), becoming its president. Upon Nkrumah’s arrival in London in 1945, Adjei hosted him at his home until he found accommodation and introduced him to WASU members, including Kankam Boadu, Joe Appiah, and Kojo Botsio. Together, they organized the Fifth Pan-African Congress in Manchester in 1945, which was attended by W. E. B. Du Bois, Hastings Banda, and Jomo Kenyatta and is regarded as a turning point in the independence struggle. Adjei enrolled at the London School of Economics and Political Science for an M.Sc. degree while studying law at the Inner Temple, though his dissertation on "The Dynamics of Social Change" was not completed due to time constraints. He passed all bar examinations and was called to the Bar at the Inner Temple in January 1947. Returning to the Gold Coast in May 1947, he enrolled at the Ghana bar and initially intended to launch a chain of newspapers to promote self-rule, but due to financial constraints, he joined Adumoa-Bossman and Co. chambers as a legal practitioner. He met J. B. Danquah, who was discussing the formation of a national political movement, and within four days joined a meeting of the UGCC Planning Committee. He became a member of the committee and, on 4 August 1947, one of the leading members when the UGCC was inaugurated at Saltpond. On 22 August 1947, the Accra branch was inaugurated, with Edward Akufo-Addo as president and Emmanuel Obetsebi-Lamptey and J. Quist-Therson as vice-presidents. As the movement grew, the leaders decided to convert it into a political party and needed a full-time secretary. J. B. Danquah recommended Ako Adjei, but he declined to focus on his newspaper and legal practice, instead suggesting Kwame Nkrumah, who was then running the West African National Secretariat (WANS) in London. Adjei recommended Nkrumah because he had observed his organizational skills and had been assured by Nkrumah that he would return to London after gaining experience in Ghana. Adjei wrote to Nkrumah and sent him £100, provided by George Alfred Grant, the UGCC’s founder and financier, for his trip to the Gold Coast. Upon Nkrumah’s arrival in December 1947, Adjei introduced him to key UGCC members, including G. A. Grant, J. B. Danquah, and R. S. Blay. As general-secretary, Nkrumah began expanding the UGCC’s reach and focused on the plight of ex-servicemen, who had not received their emoluments after World War II. The UGCC lawyers helped draft a petition to the governor, which was presented on 24 February 1948, coinciding with the Nii Kwabena Bonnie III-led boycott campaign and resulting in the 1948 Accra Riots. As a result, Ako Adjei and other UGCC leaders, including J. B. Danquah, Emmanuel Obetsebi-Lamptey, Edward Akufo-Addo, William Ofori Atta, and Kwame Nkrumah, were arrested and blamed by the British government for the unrest, with Adjei detained at Navrongo. The release of the Big Six led to a split between Nkrumah and the UGCC, with Nkrumah forming the Convention People's Party (CPP) in 1949. Ako Adjei remained with the UGCC and later criticized Nkrumah in his newspapers, the African National Times and the Star of Ghana. In the 1951 Gold Coast legislative election, he stood for the UGCC in the Accra Central Municipal Electoral District, polling 1,451 votes compared to Nkrumah’s 20,780 and Emmanuel Obetsebi-Lamptey’s 1,630. After the UGCC’s poor performance, he joined efforts to merge opposition parties and became Secretary of the Ghana Congress Party (GCP) in May 1952. He later refused to attend meetings due to criticism over introducing Nkrumah to dismantle the UGCC. In March 1953, under pressure from E. C. Quaye, Sonny Provençal, and Paul Tagoe, he joined the CPP and delivered his first speech at a major rally in Accra. In the 1954 Gold Coast legislative election, he ran for the CPP in Accra East, polling 11,660 votes against Nai Tete’s 768, Kwamla Armah-Kwarteng’s 471, and Nii Kwabena Bonnie III’s 317, and entered parliament on 15 June 1954. On 28 July 1954, he was appointed Minister of Trade and Labour by Prime Minister Kwame Nkrumah, a move intended to include middle-class professionals in the CPP. As Minister of Trade and Labour, he oversaw the Agricultural Produce Marketing Board, the Cocoa Marketing Board, the Industrial Development Corporation, Trade Unions, and Cooperatives. On 29 February 1956, he was appointed Minister for Interior and Justice, a position previously held by Archie Casely-Hayford, and was re-elected in the 1956 Gold Coast legislative election to represent Accra East. Following Ghana’s independence on 6 March 1957, major cabinet appointments were made by Prime Minister Dr. Kwame Nkrumah. After his release in 1966, Ako Adjei lived in relative obscurity, focusing on his family and legal career. In 1992, he published a biography of George Grant. In 1997, he was awarded the Order of the Star of Ghana, the highest national honor in Ghana, for his contributions to the independence struggle. He died after a short illness in 2002.

Ako Adjei was appointed a member of the Gold Coast cabinet on 28 July 1954 by Prime Minister Dr. Kwame Nkrumah, serving as Minister of Trade and Labour. This appointment was partly due to his status as a middle-class intellectual and professional, a move seen as a strategy to attract such individuals to the CPP. As Minister of Trade and Labour, he oversaw the Agricultural Produce Marketing Board, the Cocoa Marketing Board, the Industrial Development Corporation, Trade Unions, and Cooperatives. On 29 February 1956, he was appointed Minister for Interior and Justice, a position previously held by Archie Casely-Hayford; he was also re-elected in the 1956 Gold Coast legislative election to represent the Accra East district. Following Ghana's independence on 6 March 1957, Ako Adjei remained in the Ministry of Interior and Justice, which was split in August 1957 into separate ministries, with Ako Adjei becoming Minister of Justice. It was rumored that Nkrumah made this change because Ako Adjei, though Ga, was considered "too gentlemanly" to manage the Ga-Adangbe Shifimo Kpee, a tribal organization active in Accra. Supporters believed he was better suited to handle judicial matters as a trained lawyer, and as Minister of Justice, he managed the Land Boundaries Settlement Commission, financial and ministerial affairs related to the Supreme Court, local courts, and customary law, and foreign processes. In 1958, he was moved to the Ministry of Labour and Cooperatives, where he helped establish labor structures that continue to exist and led Ghanaian delegations to the United Nations. In February 1959, he replaced Nathaniel Azarco Welbeck as Resident Minister of Guinea and was appointed Minister of External Affairs in April of the same year, holding both positions until September 1959 when he was relieved of his duties in Guinea and replaced by J. H. Allassani. On 8 April 1961, Nkrumah announced the removal of African Affairs from the Ministry of External Affairs and appointed Imoru Egala as Minister of State for African Affairs, a position without a successor. Ako Adjei returned to Ghana to argue for a more coordinated foreign policy, believing African unity would fail without integration of African relations under his ministry, but his efforts were unsuccessful. In May 1961, the portfolio was renamed Minister of Foreign Affairs, making Ako Adjei Ghana’s first Minister of Foreign Affairs in the first republic. He played a key role in shaping Ghana’s foreign policy during the Cold War, presenting a sober image of Ghana at international forums and advocating for a Union of African States, an Africa Customs Union, an Africa Free Trade Zone, and an Africa Development Fund—proposals later adopted by the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) and the Africa Union (AU). He announced a complete boycott of South African goods, ships, and airlines, allowing entry only to those who opposed apartheid. Ako Adjei remained Minister of Foreign Affairs until August 1962 when he was charged with treason in connection with the Kulungugu bomb attack on 1 August 1962, a failed assassination attempt on President Nkrumah. He, along with Tawia Adamafio and Hugh Horatio Cofie Crabbe, were accused of plotting the assassination. The Supreme Court acquitted them, citing circumstantial and fraudulent evidence, with the basis of the accusation centered on internal CPP dissensions. A member of Parliament, F. E. Techie Menson, described their actions during the incident as isolating themselves from the President and riding in separate vehicles. The three judges who acquitted them—Justice Sir Kobina Arku Korsah, Justice Edward Akufo-Addo, and Justice Kofi Adumua Bossman—were forced to resign, and two other judges, William Bedford Van Lare and Robert Samuel Blay, were dismissed for protesting. Nkrumah then appointed a 12-man jury headed by Justice Julius Sarkodee-Addo, which found the three guilty based on the testimony of a fetish priest. Ako Adjei and the others were sentenced to death, later commuted to life imprisonment and then to 20 years by a presidential address on 26 March 1965. Ako Adjei stated he was innocent and that Adamafio and Cofie Crabbe were also innocent, recounting that he accompanied Nkrumah to a meeting with Upper Volta’s President Maurice Yameogo on 31 July 1962, and that during the return journey, a grenade was thrown at the President after he stopped to receive a bouquet from a boy at Kulungugu, killing the boy and injuring the President. He was arrested on 29 August 1962, during a reception for a visitor, and remained in detention for four years. Ako Adjei, along with his colleagues, was released by the National Liberation Council after the 24 February 1966 military coup that overthrew Nkrumah. He was released from Nsawam Medium Security Prison on 6 September 1966. After his release, he completely forswore politics, dedicating himself to his family and legal practice, reorganizing his chambers, Teianshi Chambers, and resuming private legal work. In 1978, he was appointed to a constitutional drafting commission by the Supreme Military Council for the Third Republic. The last time he was seen in a high-profile gathering was during a senior citizens event organized by former President Rawlings, though his relatives denied interviews due to his health. Ako Adjei was the last surviving member of the Big Six and died on 14 January 2002 at the age of 85 at Korle-Bu Teaching Hospital, survived by his wife and four children. His death drew tributes from leaders including President John Agyekum Kufour, who declared a state burial, stating that the nation owes him gratitude for advancing democratic rule and that the era of the Big Six had ended but their legacy remains. President Nana Akufo-Addo noted that the death marked the end of the founding fathers’ era and that their vision for free democratic rule now prevails. Jake Obetsebi-Lamptey emphasized that the chapter of the Big Six has not been erased and that their experiences are valuable for future generations. On the day of burial, all flags flew at half-mast; the state funeral was held at the state house, attended by politicians, ministers, diplomats, chiefs, relatives, and sympathizers. Wreaths were laid by President Kufour, Minister Hackman Owusu-Agyeman, President of the Ghana Bar Association Paul Adu-Gyamfi, and a family member. Joseph Henry Mensah read the government tribute, stating that Ako Adjei was a key figure in articulating African unity and bridging the CPP and UGCC, and lamenting that Ghana lost a gem whose wisdom could have been fully utilized. A private burial followed at the Holy Church of God, Okoman, Dome, in Accra. Ako Adjei was married to Theodosia Ako Adjei (née Kote-Amon), with whom he had four daughters. He was a Christian and a member of the Presbyterian Church of Ghana, believing that God controls all affairs and that individuals should serve Him as tools. The Ako Adjei Interchange in Accra (formerly Sankara Interchange) and Ako-Adjei Park in Osu, Accra, are named in his honor. He once said, "Ghana is our country. We have nowhere to go. This is where God has placed us and the earlier we realized this the better for all of us."
